title: Episode 28: Branch Protection and Rulesets
description: Required reviews, status checks, rulesets, and diagnosing blocked merges.
concepts: Why branch protection exists: preventing accidental changes to main
Branch protection rules: the classic approach
Required pull request reviews before merging
Required status checks: CI must pass before merge
Restricting who can push to the branch
Rulesets: the newer, more flexible approach
Rulesets versus branch protection rules: key differences
Creating a ruleset with tag and branch patterns
Diagnosing why a push is rejected or a merge is blocked
Bypass lists: allowing specific people or apps to bypass rules
Common configurations: small team, open source project, enterprise
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we’re unpacking one of the most common GitHub mysteries: you open a pull request, everything looks fine, and yet the merge button is disabled.

[JAMIE]
That moment where GitHub seems to be saying, no, but not in a very friendly tone.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And the good news is that it usually is telling you why. This lesson is for contributors trying to understand why a PR is blocked, and for workshop facilitators or maintainers who need to configure these rules in practice repositories.

[JAMIE]
And since this series is built for blind and low-vision learners too, we’re also going to cover how those merge requirements show up with a screen reader, what to listen for, and where the important controls live.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
At a high level, branch protection is a quality gate for important branches, usually `main`. A branch protection rule is a set of requirements that must be satisfied before a pull request can be merged.

[JAMIE]
So this is not Git being difficult for fun. It’s there to protect the project.

[ALEX]
Right. Branch protection can require code review before changes enter the default branch. It can require automated tests to pass. It can prevent direct pushes to `main` so work has to come through pull requests. It can require your branch to be current with the latest `main`. And in some repositories, it can require commits to be signed.

[JAMIE]
So when a learner says, my PR won’t merge, one likely answer is: the repository is enforcing standards, not rejecting you personally.

[ALEX]
Well said.

[JAMIE]
Can we make this concrete for navigation? If someone is on a pull request page, where do these rules actually surface?

[ALEX]
Usually in the merge box near the bottom of the PR conversation view. For screen reader users, one practical strategy is to press End to jump to the bottom, then navigate by heading to find the merge area. The status lines just above the merge button explain what’s missing. You might hear things like, one review required, some checks haven’t completed yet, or this branch is out of date.

[JAMIE]
And if the merge button is disabled or announced as unavailable, don’t stop there. The explanation is usually right above it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. For low-vision users, the merge area also uses color and small status icons: green for ready, yellow for pending, red for blocked. Zooming in can help a lot, especially because buttons like Update branch or links like Show all checks can be easy to miss at high magnification if you’re scanning quickly.

[JAMIE]
And for sighted users, same idea: bottom of the PR conversation tab, look above the merge button, read the checklist, expand checks if needed.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let’s talk through the most common branch protection rules.

[JAMIE]
First up: reviews.

[ALEX]
Required reviews are probably the most common rule. A maintainer can say that a pull request needs one or more approving reviews before it can be merged.

[JAMIE]
So if the repository says require one approving review, the merge box might literally tell me one review required.

[ALEX]
Yes. And there are a couple of details learners often miss. If a reviewer requests changes, that does not count as approval. Also, if you push new commits after approval, some repositories dismiss stale reviews automatically. That means previous approvals are withdrawn and you need a fresh approval after the latest changes.

[JAMIE]
That prevents a bad pattern where someone gets approval and then sneaks in extra changes after the review.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And if you do push a fix, it’s good practice to re-request review from the original reviewer.

[JAMIE]
What about automated checks?

[ALEX]
That’s the next big category: required status checks. These are automated workflows, often GitHub Actions, but they can also come from third-party services. The repository can require those checks to succeed before merging is allowed.

[JAMIE]
What are some example check names a learner might encounter?

[ALEX]
Things like `ci / build`, which compiles the code. `ci / test`, which runs tests. `lint`, which checks formatting or code style. `accessibility-check`, for automated accessibility scanning. `CodeQL`, for security analysis. Or something like `netlify/deploy-preview`, where a preview site has to build successfully.

[JAMIE]
And required means not optional. If a required check is failing or still running, merge is blocked.

[ALEX]
Correct.

[JAMIE]
Another one people see a lot is being out of date with the base branch.

[ALEX]
Yes. Some repositories require your branch to be up to date before merge. If new commits landed on `main` after you created your branch, the merge box may say this branch is out of date with the base branch.

[JAMIE]
And then there may be an Update branch button.

[ALEX]
Right. Clicking Update branch tells GitHub to merge current `main` into your branch. Some teams may prefer a rebase workflow instead, but that depends on project policy and your comfort level.

[JAMIE]
Then we have signed commits.

[ALEX]
If a repository requires signed commits, every commit in the PR must show as verified. That usually means GPG or SSH signing is configured correctly. If commits are unverified, the PR cannot be merged until you create signed commits instead.

[JAMIE]
And linear history?

[ALEX]
That rule means the repository wants a clean, non-branchy history. No merge commits into the protected branch. So maintainers may only allow squash merges or rebase merges.

[JAMIE]
So if I see a message that the repository requires a linear history, it usually means the eventual merge strategy must avoid a merge commit.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[JAMIE]
And lock branch sounds even stricter.

[ALEX]
It is. A locked branch is effectively read-only. No merges go in. Maintainers might do this for archived repositories or temporary release freezes.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now, there’s a newer concept here too: rulesets.

[ALEX]
Yes. Repository rulesets are the modern evolution of branch protection. Classic branch protection still exists and is still very common, but rulesets are more flexible.

[JAMIE]
What do they add?

[ALEX]
They can apply rules at the organization level across many repositories, not just one repo and one branch. They support bypass lists, so specific users, roles, or automation accounts can be exempted. They can target branch patterns like `release/*` or `v*`. They provide violation insights, which help admins audit when rules were bypassed. And they support enforcement modes such as active, evaluate, and disabled.

[JAMIE]
Evaluate is interesting. That means log violations without actually blocking people yet.

[ALEX]
Exactly. It’s useful when an organization wants to test a policy before enforcing it.

[JAMIE]
Can you compare classic branch protection and rulesets in plain language?

[ALEX]
Classic branch protection is narrower: typically one branch in one repository, no real bypass list, active enforcement only. Rulesets are broader and more modern: multiple branches, patterns, organization-wide use, configurable bypass, and multiple enforcement modes.

[JAMIE]
But for most learners contributing to public repositories, they’ll still often encounter classic branch protection.

[ALEX]
Yes. Many repos still use it. And importantly, contributors usually do not need admin access to understand what’s happening. The merge box messages usually tell you enough.

[JAMIE]
If someone does have access and wants to inspect rulesets, where would they look?

[ALEX]
Typically in a repository’s Insights tab under Rulesets, if visible to them, or in Settings, then Rules, then Rulesets, which is generally admin-only.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let’s move into diagnosis mode. Suppose your PR cannot be merged. How do you read the message and decide what to do?

[JAMIE]
Let’s do the common messages one by one.

[ALEX]
If the merge area says something like one review required or two reviews required, the meaning is straightforward: you do not yet have the required number of approvals.

[JAMIE]
So what should the contributor do?

[ALEX]
Request review from the right people, often a maintainer or code owner. Check whether someone requested changes, because that can block approval. Wait for the reviewer to submit their review. If you respond by pushing new commits, re-request review afterward.

[JAMIE]
Next: some checks haven’t completed yet, or some checks were not successful.

[ALEX]
That means at least one required status check is pending or failing. The next step is to expand the checks list, often through a Show all checks control, identify the failing check, and open its Details link to read the full log.

[JAMIE]
And then fix the actual problem, not the symptom.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Maybe a test failed. Maybe linting found formatting issues. Maybe the build broke. Maybe an accessibility scan found a violation. Push a new commit with the fix, and the checks usually re-run automatically.

[JAMIE]
How long should someone expect to wait?

[ALEX]
Often one to five minutes, though it varies. If checks pass on `main` but fail on your PR, that strongly suggests the issue is specific to your changes. And if a check has been stuck in progress for a long time, say over thirty minutes, the workflow runner or service may have a problem. At that point, contact the maintainer.

[JAMIE]
Next message: this branch is out of date with the base branch.

[ALEX]
That means new commits reached `main` and your branch no longer includes them. The easiest fix may be the Update branch button in the merge box. Or, if you’re comfortable and the project permits it, you can update locally with fetch and rebase, then force-push carefully.

[JAMIE]
And the signed commits message?

[ALEX]
If the message says commits must have verified signatures, your commits are not signed in the required way. The fix is not usually a button on the PR page. You need to configure commit signing properly, then re-create or amend the commits so GitHub recognizes them as verified.

[JAMIE]
And then there’s the more generic message: merging is blocked.

[ALEX]
That one often means there are multiple unmet rules or a broader ruleset restriction. Read every status line in the merge box. Don’t assume there is only one problem. There may be a missing review and a failing check, for example.

[JAMIE]
So the general method is: read the exact text, identify whether the blocker is people, automation, branch freshness, commit verification, or repository policy, then take the next action that matches that category.

[ALEX]
Perfect summary.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let’s spend real time on accessibility and the merge box, because this is where a lot of frustration happens.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. If you’re using a screen reader, start by getting to the lower part of the pull request page. Pressing End is often the fastest route. Then navigate by headings or landmarks until you reach the merge area.

[JAMIE]
What should the learner listen for once they’re there?

[ALEX]
Listen for status text before the button itself. The merge box is not just a button area. It is an explanation area. You may hear whether the PR is ready to merge, blocked, waiting on checks, or waiting on review.

[JAMIE]
Can we mention specific screen reader workflows?

[ALEX]
Yes, while keeping in mind that GitHub’s interface evolves. For NVDA users, browse mode with heading navigation is often effective. Jump to the bottom, then use H to move through headings near the merge section, and arrow through the status text and controls like Show all checks, Details, Update branch, or the merge button.

[JAMIE]
And for JAWS?

[ALEX]
A similar strategy works: move to the bottom, use heading navigation or the links list and buttons list as needed, then read line by line around the merge controls. If the button is unavailable, keep reading nearby text because the explanation is usually adjacent.

[JAMIE]
So regardless of screen reader, the principle is: don’t just tab until you hit a disabled button and stop. Explore the surrounding text.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[JAMIE]
How do status checks fit into that navigation?

[ALEX]
Look for controls that expand the checks summary, often labeled Show all checks. Once expanded, each check may have a name, a state, and a Details link. The state might indicate passing, failing, pending, or cancelled.

[JAMIE]
And reading check details means opening the detailed log for the failing job.

[ALEX]
Yes. That’s where you learn whether the issue is a failed test, a dependency install problem, a style violation, a deployment error, or something else.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let’s broaden from merge box mechanics to the concept of status checks themselves.

[ALEX]
A status check is a reported result attached to your commit or pull request. It tells GitHub whether some automated process succeeded, failed, is still running, or did not run successfully enough for the repository’s rules.

[JAMIE]
And many of these come from GitHub Actions.

[ALEX]
Right. GitHub Actions is GitHub’s built-in automation system. A repository can include workflow files under `.github/workflows`, and one common example is a file like `ci.yml`.

[JAMIE]
Which usually means continuous integration.

[ALEX]
Exactly. A CI workflow might run when you push commits or open a pull request. It may check out the code, install dependencies, build the project, run tests, run linters, maybe run accessibility or security checks, and then report the result back to GitHub as status checks.

[JAMIE]
So when a learner sees something like `ci / test`, that’s probably one job inside a workflow file, not some mysterious separate system.

[ALEX]
Correct. Though not all checks come from GitHub Actions. Some come from third-party services, like external CI platforms, deployment previews, security scanners, or code quality services.

[JAMIE]
What are the main states a learner should recognize?

[ALEX]
Passing or successful, which usually shows a green indicator. Pending or in progress, often a spinner or waiting state. Failing or unsuccessful, usually marked in red. You may also encounter cancelled, skipped, or neutral states, though whether those block merge depends on repository configuration and whether the check is required.

[JAMIE]
So the key question is not just did a check run, but is it required, and what state is it in.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Who can actually configure all this?

[ALEX]
Usually repository administrators, maintainers with the right permissions, or organization owners for org-level rulesets. Regular contributors generally cannot change branch protection. They can only comply with it.

[JAMIE]
Which is useful emotionally too. If you’re blocked by a rule, it does not mean you’re expected to fix the repository settings yourself.

[ALEX]
Right. Your job is to understand the rule, satisfy it if you can, and ask a maintainer when the blocker is infrastructural or administrative.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we wrap up, can we give a practical workshop-oriented reference setup? What might a training repository enforce?

[ALEX]
A workshop repository often enables a simple but realistic set of protections on `main`: require at least one approving review, require key status checks like build or test to pass, prevent direct pushes to `main`, and sometimes require the branch to be up to date before merging.

[JAMIE]
Usually not every advanced rule all at once.

[ALEX]
Right. For teaching, you want enough realism to show the workflow, but not so many restrictions that learners spend the whole session debugging policy instead of learning GitHub.

[JAMIE]
And that also helps facilitators explain why a pull request may be blocked in a controlled, understandable way.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let me try a compact recap. Branch protection is the repository’s quality gate for important branches. Common blockers are missing reviews, failing or pending checks, an out-of-date branch, unsigned commits, linear-history rules, or a locked branch. Modern repositories may use rulesets, which are more flexible than classic branch protection. And for accessibility, the merge box is the key area to inspect, especially the status text above the button.

[ALEX]
That’s it. And one final note: if you want the most authoritative details, GitHub’s documentation on protected branches and rulesets is the source to trust, because exact UI wording and available options can change over time.

[JAMIE]
So when your merge button is greyed out, treat it like feedback, not failure.

[ALEX]
Well said. Read the message, identify the category of blocker, take the matching next step, and you’ll usually get unstuck quickly.

[JAMIE]
And if not, you’ll at least know what question to ask a maintainer.

[ALEX]
Exactly. That’s a strong open source skill.

# Appendix O: Branch Protection Rules and Repository Rulesets
>
> **Listen to Episode 28:** [Branch Protection and Rulesets](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Reference companion to:** [Chapter 08: Open Source Culture](08-open-source-culture.md) | Also relevant: [Chapter 14](14-git-in-practice.md)
>
> **Authoritative source:** [GitHub Docs: Protected branches](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches)

## How Merging Rules Work and Why Your PR May Be Blocked

> **Who this is for:** Contributors who have submitted a PR and are wondering why it cannot be merged yet, as well as workshop facilitators who configure branch protection for practice repositories.

## Quick Navigation

1. [What Branch Protection Does](#1-what-branch-protection-does)
2. [Common Branch Protection Rules](#2-common-branch-protection-rules)
3. [Repository Rulesets - The Modern Approach](#3-repository-rulesets---the-modern-approach)
4. [Why Your PR Cannot Be Merged - Diagnosis Guide](#4-why-your-pr-cannot-be-merged---diagnosis-guide)
5. [Navigating the Merge Box with a Screen Reader](#5-navigating-the-merge-box-with-a-screen-reader)
6. [Status Checks - What They Are and What They Mean](#6-status-checks---what-they-are-and-what-they-mean)
7. [Who Can Configure Branch Protection](#7-who-can-configure-branch-protection)
8. [Workshop Repository Configuration Reference](#8-workshop-repository-configuration-reference)

## 1. What Branch Protection Does

A **branch protection rule** is a set of requirements that must be satisfied before a PR can be merged into a specific branch (typically `main`). Branch protection exists to:

- Require that code is reviewed before it enters the default branch
- Require that automated tests pass before merging
- Prevent direct pushes to `main` without a PR
- Ensure the branch is up-to-date before merging
- Require commits to be signed (GPG or SSH signatures)

Think of branch protection as the quality gate for a repository's primary branch.

### Learning Cards: What Branch Protection Does

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- The merge box at the bottom of every PR page is where branch protection surfaces its requirements — press End to jump to the bottom, then use H to find the merge heading
- Each requirement is announced as a status line: "1 review required," "Some checks haven't completed yet," etc. — listen for these before attempting to merge
- If the Merge button says "disabled" or "grayed out," branch protection is blocking — the status lines immediately above explain exactly what is needed

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- The merge box uses green (ready), yellow (pending), and red (blocked) indicators — zoom in on the merge area to read the text labels next to each colored icon
- The "Update branch" button appears as a secondary button above the merge button when your PR is behind main — it can be easy to miss at high zoom
- Required checks show checkmark or X icons that are small at default size — browser zoom to 150%+ makes the pass/fail status easier to distinguish

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- Look at the bottom of the PR Conversation tab for the merge box — a green "Merge pull request" button means all requirements are met; grey means something is blocking
- The list of requirements appears as a vertical checklist above the merge button — each item shows a green checkmark, yellow spinner, or red X
- Click "Show all checks" to expand the full list of status checks if only a summary is visible

</details>

## 2. Common Branch Protection Rules

### Required Reviews

The most common rule. The maintainer requires a minimum number of approving reviews before the PR can be merged.

**Example:** "Require 1 approving review"

What this means for you:

- Your PR shows a "1 review required" notice in the merge box
- If a reviewer requests changes, their approval is revoked - you need at least one new approval after your latest push
- After you push new commits, re-request review from the original reviewer

**Dismiss stale reviews:** Some repos have this enabled - whenever you push a new commit, all existing approvals are automatically withdrawn and you need a fresh review. This prevents sneaking in bad code after approval.

### Required Status Checks

Automated workflows (GitHub Actions or third-party CI) must complete successfully before merging is allowed.

#### Example checks you may see

- `ci / build` - compiles the code
- `ci / test` - runs the test suite
- `lint` - code style checks
- `accessibility-check` - automated accessibility scanning
- `CodeQL` - security analysis
- `netlify/deploy-preview` - preview deployment must succeed

**What "Required" means:** The merge button is grayed out (or shows an error) until all required checks show a green checkmark. A failing or pending check blocks the merge.

### Require Branches to Be Up to Date

Before merging, your PR branch must include all changes from `main`. This prevents merge conflicts from being introduced silently.

If your PR is behind `main`:

- The merge box shows: "This branch is out of date with the base branch"
- Button: "Update branch" - merges current `main` into your branch
- Alternative: Rebase your branch (only if the maintainer permits rebase merges)

### Require Signed Commits

All commits in the PR must have a Verified badge (see [Appendix D: Git Authentication](appendix-d-git-authentication.md)). If your commits are unverified, the PR cannot be merged until you re-commit with signing enabled.

### Require Linear History

Only squash merges or rebase merges are permitted - no merge commits. This keeps the commit history linear and readable.

If you see: "This repository requires a linear history" - the maintainer will squash or rebase merge your PR, not create a merge commit.

### Lock Branch

A locked branch cannot receive any merges - it is effectively read-only. This is sometimes used for archived repositories or during release freezes.

## 3. Repository Rulesets - The Modern Approach

**Repository Rulesets** (introduced in late 2023) are the next generation of branch protection. They extend branch protection rules with:

- **Organization-level rules** - apply across all repos in an org from one place
- **Bypass lists** - specific users or roles can be exempted from rules (e.g., release bots)
- **Target multiple branches** - one ruleset can target a pattern like `release/*` or `v*`
- **Violation insights** - audit log of when rules were bypassed and by whom
- **Rule enforcement** - Active (enforced), Evaluate (only log violations, don't block), Disabled

### Rulesets vs. Branch Protection Rules

| Feature | Branch Protection Rules | Repository Rulesets |
| ---------  | ------------------------  | ---------------------  |
| Scope | Single branch, single repo | Patterns, multi-branch, cross-org |
| Bypass | No bypass capability | Configurable bypass list |
| Enforcement modes | Active only | Active, Evaluate, Disabled |
| Organization-level | No | Yes (org rulesets) |
| Status | Classic (still supported) | Current/modern approach |

Most repositories you encounter still use classic branch protection rules. Rulesets will become more common as maintainers migrate.

### Finding and Reading Rulesets

If you want to understand why certain rules apply to a branch:

```text
Repository → Insights tab → Rulesets (if you have access - contributors usually don't)
Or: Repository → Settings → Rules → Rulesets (admin only)
```

Alternatively, PR merge box messages describe which rules are blocking - you don't need admin access to understand what's required.

## 4. Why Your PR Cannot Be Merged - Diagnosis Guide

When you open a PR and the merge button is grayed out or shows an error, the merge box tells you exactly what needs to happen. Here is how to read it.

### "X review required / X reviews required"

**What it means:** The required number of approvals hasn't been reached yet.

#### What to do

1. Request review from a codeowner or maintainer (right sidebar → Reviewers → request)
2. Check if any reviews exist but requested changes - those count against you
3. Wait for the reviewer to submit their review
4. Respond to requested changes by pushing new commits, then re-requesting review

### "Some checks haven't completed yet" or "Some checks were not successful"

**What it means:** A required status check is pending or failing.

#### What to do

1. Scroll down to the merge box - expand "Show all checks"
2. Find the failing check → click "Details" to see the full log
3. Fix the underlying issue (test failure, lint error, build error) in your branch
4. Push new commits - checks re-run automatically
5. Wait for checks to complete (typically 1-5 minutes for most CI)

**If checks pass on `main` but fail on your PR:** The issue is specific to your changes. Read the check log carefully.

**If checks are stuck "in progress" for over 30 minutes:** The workflow runner may have an issue - contact the maintainer.

### "This branch is out of date with the base branch"

**What it means:** New commits were pushed to `main` after you created your PR branch. The maintainer requires everything to be current.

#### What to do

- Click **"Update branch"** in the merge box - GitHub does a merge commit from `main` into your branch
- Or locally: `git fetch upstream && git rebase upstream/main` then force-push (only if you are comfortable with rebase)

### "Commits must have verified signatures"

**What it means:** Branch protection requires signed commits (see [Appendix D: Git Authentication](appendix-d-git-authentication.md)).

#### What to do

1. Enable commit signing locally before making more commits
2. For existing unsigned commits, you need to rebase-rewrite them - this is advanced; ask the maintainer if there is a workaround

### "Merging is blocked"

**What it means:** A ruleset or branch protection has explicitly blocked merging for a reason not covered by other messages. Check the PR for a pinned comment from the mergeable status check or a GitHub Actions check that posts a comment explaining the block.

### Learning Cards: Why Your PR Cannot Be Merged

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- Navigate to the merge box (End key, then H key to find "Merge" heading) and read each status line with arrow keys — the messages tell you exactly what action to take
- When a check fails, Tab to the "Details" link next to the failing check name and press Enter to open the log — use Ctrl+F to search for "error" or "failed"
- After pushing a fix, the checks re-run automatically — return to the PR page and listen for the status to change from "pending" to "passed"

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- Failed checks show a red X icon that can be tiny — zoom to 150%+ and look for the word "failing" or "failed" next to each check name
- The "Update branch" button (for out-of-date PRs) is a secondary action that blends in at low zoom — look for it directly above the main merge button
- The Details link next to each check opens a log page with monospace text — increase your editor or browser font size before reading long CI logs

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- Scroll to the bottom of the PR page and scan the checklist in the merge box — red X items are blocking, yellow spinners are still running, green checks are done
- Click the "Details" link next to any red X to see the full error log — the failing step is highlighted with a red icon in the left sidebar
- If "This branch is out of date," click the blue "Update branch" button and wait for checks to re-run before merging

</details>

## 5. Navigating the Merge Box with a Screen Reader

The merge box lives at the bottom of every PR page. With a screen reader, navigating to it efficiently is important.

### Reaching the Merge Box

```text
PR page → End key (jump to bottom of page)
Or: B key (NVDA Browse Mode) → navigate buttons → look for "Merge pull request" button
Or: H key → navigate to "Merge" heading area
```

### Reading the Merge Box Status

```text
From the merge box area:
H → section heading ("Merging is blocked" or "This branch has no conflicts")
↓ → first status message
↓/Tab → each requirement listed (required reviews, required checks, etc.)
```

#### NVDA specific path

```text
NVDA+F7 → Elements list → Filter by type: Headings
Find "Merge" related heading → move focus to that section
Then ↓ through the section content
```

#### JAWS specific path

```text
H → navigate to merge section
Then ↓ key → read each item in the requirements list
```

### Checking Status Checks

```text
Merge box area → Tab → "Show all checks" link or button → Enter
Expands to show: each check name, its status (passed/failed/pending), "Details" link
Tab through each check → "Details" link → Enter to open the check log
```

### Reading Check Details

The check log is a text-heavy page in a pre-formatted block.

```text
Check log page: H → "Summary" heading → ↓ to read summary
To read the full log: F → form controls → step dropdown (if multi-step)
Or: Tab → each step accordion → Enter to expand → ↓ to read log lines
Log content is usually in a scrollable region: ↓ key scrolls through lines
```

## 6. Status Checks - What They Are and What They Mean

Status checks come from two sources:

### GitHub Actions Status Checks

Defined in `.github/workflows/*.yml` in the repository. Each `job:` in a workflow file becomes a status check. Example:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
jobs:
  test:           ← this creates the "test" status check
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test
```

### Third-Party Status Checks

Services like Netlify, Vercel, Codecov, and Snyk post status checks via the GitHub API. You will recognize them by their app name prefix (e.g., `netlify/deploy-preview - Deploy Preview ready`).

### Status Check States

| Icon | State | Meaning |
| ------  | -------  | ---------  |
| Yellow circle | Pending | Running now or queued |
| Green checkmark | Success | Passed, no issues |
| Red X | Failure | Failed - PR cannot be merged until fixed |
| Red circle | Error | Unexpected error in the check runner (not your code's fault) |
| Grey circle | Skipped | Not relevant for this PR (conditional run) |
| Neutral | Neutral | Informational - does not block merge |

## 7. Who Can Configure Branch Protection

| Role | Can view requirements | Can modify requirements |
| ------  | -----------------------  | -------------------------  |
| Public viewer | No (only via PR merge box) | No |
| Contributor | PR merge box only | No |
| Triage | PR merge box only | No |
| Write | Settings → Rules (read-only in most cases) | No |
| Maintain | Yes | Partial |
| Admin | Yes | Yes - full control |
| Org admin | Yes | Yes - including org-level rulesets |

As a workshop participant, you are typically a **contributor** to the main `community-access/accessibility-agents` repo and an **admin** of your own fork. On your fork, you can configure branch protection however you like - including disabling it entirely for practice purposes.

## 8. Workshop Repository Configuration Reference

The `community-access/accessibility-agents` repository uses the following branch protection configuration on `main`:

| Rule | Setting |
| ------  | ---------  |
| Required reviews | 1 approving review |
| Dismiss stale reviews | Yes - new commits require re-review |
| Require status checks | `ci / build` and `ci / test` |
| Up-to-date requirement | Yes |
| Signed commits | No (to reduce friction for workshop participants) |
| Restrict direct pushes | Yes - all changes must come through PRs |

**Workshop tip:** Your personal fork of [accessibility-agents](https://github.com/Community-Access/accessibility-agents) has no branch protection by default. If you want to practice the full "review before merge" workflow with a partner, you can add branch protection to your fork:

```text
Your fork → Settings → Branches → Add branch protection rule
Branch name pattern: main
Check: Require a pull request before merging
Check: Require approvals → 1
Save changes
```

Then practice opening a PR on your fork and requesting your workshop partner's review.

Welcome back. Today we're working with one of those GitHub features that quietly makes open source collaboration much easier: issue templates.

[JAMIE]
And this is a great one for people who have ever opened a blank issue form and thought, what exactly am I supposed to put here?

[ALEX]
Exactly. An issue template turns that blank box into a guided experience. Instead of guessing what maintainers need, contributors get prompts, structure, and clear required fields. That reduces back-and-forth, improves quality, and helps teams act on issues faster.

[JAMIE]
So this is not just about formatting. It's about making contributions clearer and more usable.

[ALEX]
Yes, and especially in accessibility work. If someone is reporting an accessibility barrier, a vague report can be hard to reproduce. A thoughtful template can ask where the problem occurred, what assistive technology was involved, what the expected behavior was, and how severe the barrier is.
